Levon Is a Quirky Skoolie That Serves as a Home Away From Home for Music-Loving Travelers
27 photos
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot
Old, decommissioned school buses turned into cozy, functional living spaces are one of the hottest trends in the realm of tiny living. With their sturdy construction, generous interior volume, and affordability compared to traditional RVs, these vehicles are seen by many as the perfect blank canvas for creating functional roving homes.
For many people, a school bus conversion is a practical way to create an affordable home on wheels, but for Dennis and Marty, it was an opportunity to turn a decades-old dream into reality and build something that echoes their personalities and everything they love about music, travel, and the freedom of the open road.
Dennis and Marty have built this quirky bus home nicknamed “Levon” not only to travel and explore new places but also to drive to music festivals all over the country. It has been their dream for 35 years. The idea of building a bus conversion first sparked in July of 1987, when Dennis attended a Grateful Dead concert in Eugene, Oregon, and saw a big converted bus that caught his attention. He then thought he had to have one of his own.
A couple of years ago, he and Marty decided it was time to make it happen. They bought a Thomas-built school bus that already had some work done to the interior and turned it into a colorful home for them and their dog, complete with an eclectic styling, plenty of unique custom features, and items that hold meaning to them.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot They worked with a couple of professionals and a talented mural artist they met at a rest area to complete the conversion, and the result is a vibrant, full-of-character skoolie and a rolling tribute to the Grateful Dead, an American rock band formed in the 1960s known for their improvisational music.
From the get-go, they wanted their build to be much more than another ordinary skoolie, and indeed, the Levon is the kind of bus you can’t miss on the highway. The exterior immediately catches the eye with a lively color scheme that is entirely inspired by the Grateful Dead. The artist created a vibrant yet cohesive artwork on the bus’s body, with all kinds of things related to the band’s music, from a steam locomotive rolling down the tracks and Mount Hood to dancing bears and a Tumbledown Shack (Grateful Dead tribute band).
The interior of the bus is just as enchanting and full of personality, if not more. The couple wanted a comfortable living space , but they didn’t follow a conventional design, so everything you see inside is custom. With a bit of creativity, audacity, and a peculiar sense of style, they created a space that speaks of their love of music.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot They used color, personal items, and an array of custom-made features to create a space where they are surrounded by things they love and that hold meaning to them. They also included every amenity they need for a comfortable life on the road.
The layout is simple and intuitive, and it flows easily from front to back with absolutely no separation walls between areas, not even for the bathroom facilities. As in many other conversions, the common, social areas occupy the front and middle of the bus, while the bathroom and sleeping quarters are toward the rear.
The entire interior is fitted with custom light blue cabinetry and furniture with lively orange cushions, and beautiful woodwork completes the design. The kitchen countertops, the dinette table, and overhead shelves are all made from live-edge natural wood, bringing a cozy, rustic touch to the space.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot The bus still preserves most of its original windows, but they like to keep the colorful curtains drawn during the day. This doesn’t mean the interior is like a dark corridor, as the beautiful wooden ceiling is dotted by no fewer than seven skylights that bathe every area in natural light.
At the front, the couple installed a comfortable leather minivan seat with harnesses, and the driver’s area is full of trinkets that move when Levon is on the move. The living area includes a custom sofa with built-in storage, while the dinette boasts booth-style seating.
The kitchen is fully functional and provides the essentials for preparing meals, but Dennis and Marty say they do most of their cooking outdoors. For sleeping, they have a huge bed at the rear, while built-in closets on either side of the bus provide plenty of storage for clothes and personal belongings.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot But the most remarkable area of the entire bus conversion is the bathroom. As mentioned, there are no walls to enclose this space, and its centerpiece is a gorgeous 1952 clawfoot bathtub, which has been given a unique makeover by a well-known Harley-Davidson tank painter.
Dennis and Marty’s love of music is reflected in many of the items they chose to decorate the interior. For instance, there are not one but two disco balls, one at the front and the other in the rear bedroom area. A drum set is also integrated on a raised section above a wheel well.
The couple doesn’t live in their bus conversion full time. Levon serves as their home away from home whenever they travel, especially when attending music festivals, but it could very well be a full-time home on wheels if they ever decide to adopt a nomadic lifestyle.
In terms of costs, Dennis and Marty paid about $67,000 for the conversion and invested another $15,000 in improvements. With the cost of the bus itself included, the project came to a total of about $90,000.
